source.title: Geometric Inductive Biases of Deep Networks: The Role of Data and Architecture
source.authors: Sajad Movahedi; Antonio Orvieto; Seyed-Mohsen Moosavi-Dezfooli

record.tranche_reason: Tests how architecture and data directions relate to generalization using geometry and test accuracy, rather than the original versions’ interventions or measures.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test accuracy for synthetic labeling tasks and data-removal comparisons. Figure-only accuracy values are not reconstructed. Random-label results report training accuracy and geometry, but not held-out accuracy. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests geometric inductive biases, but none of V1–V8 directly. Its synthetic directional tasks do not establish the convolutional advantage on image classification in V3; its removal score is not memorization as defined in V8. Random-label experiments report training accuracy and geometry without the matched held-out comparisons required by V1.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors propose that architecture constrains changes in input-space geometry during training, and present evidence linking these constraints to learnable decision boundaries, generalization, feature reliance, and sample importance.
record.recipe_differences: Studies input-space geometry and directional synthetic classification, rather than the listed random-label memorization, optimizer, batch-size, regularization, width, sharpness, or memorized-example protocols.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture and discriminant-feature direction change generalization; decision-boundary complexity, learning rate, and data size also affect reported outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Smaller eigenvalues associated with discriminant directions predict larger generalization gaps across the synthetic labeling tasks, despite 100% training accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alignment of discriminant features with initial input-space geometry predicts generalization in the tested architectures and tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Feature preference depends on geometry alignment as well as decision-boundary complexity; sufficiently misaligned linear features can lose to aligned nonlinear features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture-dependent input geometry conditions simplicity bias in synthetic classification.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing the lowest geometry-score examples retains more CIFAR-10 test accuracy than random removal; at 10% removal, the improvements are 0.9, 1.0, and 0.9 percentage points for LeNet, ResNet18, and ViT.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initial input-geometry scores can identify examples whose removal costs less accuracy than random removal.

fits_no_version.finding: The introductory concentric-circle example reports that an MLP can generalize across plane orientations while ResNet18 can fail on unfavorable orientations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Convolutional architectural biases can impair generalization on synthetic tasks whose discriminant directions are poorly aligned with those biases.

record.problems: Experiments mainly use over-parameterized models and small-scale image classification; the authors report averages without uncertainty for Figures 2, 3, and 8. Several relevant test-accuracy results are figure-only. The paper notes limited compute and does not claim results for foundation models or large-scale datasets.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 5 reports synthetic linear/non-linear component accuracy for LeNet, ResNet18, and ViT; omitted to keep rows focused on the main directional generalization result, since the text does not give recoverable numeric values. Figure 10 reports additional isotropic-data accuracy curves; values are figure-only. No held-out random-label accuracy is reported.

untested.parts: No matched demonstration of nearly perfect random-label fitting, natural-label generalization, and chance held-out random-label accuracy under the same recipe. Figures 2 and 8 also use different optimizers.
No held-out-error width sweep beyond interpolation. Figure 7 varies width to measure geometry correlations.

No direct convolutional-versus-fully-connected comparison on natural image labels establishing the claimed advantage or its local-connectivity explanation. Synthetic orientation failures address a different claim.
No controlled adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparison of held-out performance.
No controlled batch-size comparison of held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets. Appendix A.8 changes batch size with dataset size and reports training accuracy and geometry.
No dropout intervention and held-out-error comparison.
No magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation sharpness measure or comparison of its generalization-gap rankings against norms and margins. Input-space geometry is a different construct.
No removal based on an example's memorization or inclusion effect on predicting its own label.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V3 tested_not_extracted designation should be changed to not tested. States of cannot_determine for unlinked rows indicate that their measures cannot establish a listed version, not that the study's own effects are unreadable. No additional missing results bearing directly on V1–V8 were identified.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports random-label training accuracy and geometry, but does not report held-out accuracy for random labels alongside natural-label generalization.
No width sweep tests test error beyond the width needed to fit the training data.

The experiments test how architecture and discriminant-feature direction relate to generalization, but do not directly compare convolutional and fully connected networks on standard image-label tasks as V3 specifies.
The paper measures average geometry and its relation to accuracy, not magnitude-aware sharpness or a ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
The data-removal experiment ranks examples by a geometry-based score, not by memorization or their effect on predicting their own labels.

rows.value: Figure only; text states that the linear component has perfect accuracy when aligned with higher-correlation directions, while the non-linear component does not do better than a random guess.
rows.note: This is a synthetic component-learning result, not a direct comparison of convolutional and fully connected image classifiers.
rows.check: Synthetic component preference measures none of the versions. The quoted component-accuracy description is conditional on high alignment; Section 4.3 describes increasing nonlinear reliance as linear-feature alignment decreases in architectures with structured geometry. It should not be presented as an unconditional summary across directions or architectures.
